rv.q: Redgrave brings such gravity and intelligence to her performance that she makes Didion's sometimes clinical prose feel warm and immediate.
When Redgrave breaks her measured calmness and moans, "I want him back," her mouth is suddenly a black hole that no amount of magical thinking can fill.
Yet at the Booth Theater I never felt the magnetic pull that I experienced in reading the book.
With this actress portraying this writer, "The Year of Magical Thinking," which opened yesterday at the Booth, is a theatrical experience you will never forget.

The play remains, like the book, a testament to Didion’s confusion and despair and resilience and grace in trying to figure it all out, and for anyone who didn’t know the author personally, this production brings those qualities, literally, closer than ever.

Although Redgrave delivers a searing deeply felt, yet emotionally restrained performance, she is not Didion the “cool customer,” and what was so arresting about the memoir, Didion’s seemingly detached view has not been translated to the stage.

cn.t: Critics praise this "spellbinding" and "gripping" adaptation of Joan Didion's memoir, with Vanessa Redgrave delivering an arresting performance that makes the harrowing journey through grief immediate and compelling in 90 minutes of powerful theater.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
